title: Wizard Tobin and the Grumbles of the Mist
markdown:
Wizard Tobin’s beard was as full of wisdom as it was of stray crumbs from his ever-present snack pouch, and his most extraordinary companion was Mizzle. Eldoria’s mountains dared to brush the belly of the heavens, and gardens tumbled down their slopes like emerald waterfalls, tended by sprites no bigger than a thumb. Tobin was not like those showy wizards who blast bolts of lightning and stomp around with thunderous pronouncements. He was a wizard of careful planning, of neatly organised spell scrolls, and a rather impressive collection of enchanted teacups that never chipped or faded.

His greatest pride, even more than his extensive library, was Mizzle. She was a fox with eyes like polished amber, sharp and knowing, and a mind as quick as a mountain breeze through the high passes. Tobin had found her years ago, a tiny shivering ball of fluff huddled near the doorstep of his tower. He had not set out to find a familiar; he had simply offered her a warm nook by the hearth and a sliver of his favourite sharp cheese. Mizzle, in her own wise way, had chosen him. She stayed, not for his potent spells, for she was a creature of the wild and saw magic everywhere, but for the quiet kindness that hummed around him like a contented bumblebee.

On this particular morning the air was crisp and clean, smelling of fresh pine needles and the exciting promise of autumn. Tobin needed Sunpetal, a rare delicate mountain herb that bloomed only in the highest sun-drenched crevices, its petals said to capture the very essence of sunlight. He needed it for a special Elderbloom brew for the village’s grand autumn festival, a brew said to bring joy and good fortune to all who shared it.

“Mizzle, my dear,” Tobin announced, voice warm and clear as he adjusted his spectacles, which were firmly tethered to the lapels of his robes with a length of enchanted non-slip string. “Today we embark on a grand expedition for Sunpetal. I have packed provisions for a fortnight, just in case of unexpected delays, an emergency levitation charm for tricky outcrops, and, of course, a thoroughly revised edition of A Compendium of Alpine Flora with updated diagrams.”

Mizzle, busy grooming a particularly elegant paw, merely thumped her tail against the cool stone floor. Her amber eyes, however, had already scanned the overflowing satchel. And so it was plain to Mizzle that provisions for a fortnight meant a very generous, and frankly delightful, supply of fig rolls.

Their journey took them first through terraced gardens where tiny almost invisible sprites with gossamer wings tended glow-blossoms that pulsed with a soft inner light. They passed crystal lakes so pure and still you could see the pebbles on their beds winking like lost jewels. The path then wound upwards through narrow passes carved into the mountains by ancient glaciers. Here the wind sang melodies as old as the rocks themselves, a mournful yet beautiful tune. Tobin, humming a little tune of anticipation that sounded remarkably like contented hummingbirds, was quite pleased with his own foresight in bringing his sturdy hiking staff, reinforced with subtle runic carvings for extra grip.

“Ah, the Stonefang Bridge,” Tobin declared, voice carrying on the crisp mountain air as they arrived at a vast dizzying chasm. Spanning it was an old remarkably sturdy stone bridge, arches reaching out like ancient arms. The air here was noticeably cooler, and a faint mournful sound seemed to echo up from the depths below, a sound that made Mizzle’s ears prick up. And there, on a stone pillar, sat Bartholomew Crumple, a man whose moustache seemed to have a life of its own, diligently polishing a brass plaque with a vigour that could rival a mountain storm. His waistcoat was buttoned so tightly it appeared to be holding him together by sheer force of will.

“Halt,” the man boomed, though his voice cracked a little. “State your name and purpose for wishing to cross the venerable Stonefang Bridge.”

“Wizard Tobin,” Tobin replied, offering a polite nod. “And this is my valued friend, Mizzle. We are seeking Sunpetal herb, a simple gathering for the village’s autumn festival. Nothing more, I assure you.”

The guard puffed out his chest. “Simple gathering, you say? No one, and I mean no one, crosses the Stonefang Bridge without proper authorisation. I am Bartholomew Crumple, Keeper of this very Bridge, and you will require Form 7B-gamma: Declaration of Intent for Mundane Passage.” With a flourish he produced a scroll that was so long it unfurled across the ground, the size of a small tablecloth, covered in a dizzying array of boxes, intricate lines, and tiny almost microscopic print.

Tobin blinked, brow furrowing beneath his spectacles. “Form 7B-gamma? For a simple herb-gathering trip? Surely, Bartholomew, there must be some misunderstanding.”

“No misunderstanding at all,” Bartholomew huffed, moustache twitching indignantly. “Rules are rules, and this form,” he tapped it with a grubby ink-stained finger, “requires seventeen specific pieces of information. It asks for the precise weight of your intended baggage, the geological composition of your footwear, and a sworn oath that you will not engage in any unforeseen aerial acrobatics over the gorge. Most important, you see.”

Tobin was a wizard of considerable intellect, but he was also a creature of habit and exceedingly well-prepared. He rummaged contentedly in his satchel, a faint smile playing on his lips. “Ah, yes. Form 7B-gamma,” he murmured, pulling out a quill that glowed with a soft internal light, and a small unassuming inkpot that seemed to magically refill itself. “I anticipated the possibility of—”

Bureaucratic entanglements? Mizzle seemed to ask with a subtle knowing flick of her ear, nudging Tobin’s hand encouragingly.

“Precisely, my dear Mizzle.” Tobin began to fill out the form. He meticulously measured the length of his staff, scribbled down the estimated weight of his fig rolls, and swore with all due solemnity that he would remain firmly earthbound and utterly un-acrobatic.

But Mizzle was not interested in the complexities of Form 7B-gamma. Her sensitive nose twitched. She sniffed the air, then the ancient stone of the bridge, and then, with a curious tilt of her head, she sniffed Bartholomew Crumple himself. The air, which had been merely cool, was growing noticeably colder, and a strange pearly mist, thick and unnervingly silent, was beginning to drift down from the higher peaks. Tendrils of it were weaving through the dark stoic fir trees beneath a distant solitary ruined tower perched precariously on the cliff face. It swirled and coiled, not like harmless fog, but like a slumbering dragon preparing to stir. Bartholomew kept glancing nervously towards it, his vigorous polishing slowing to an anxious repetitive motion.

“Hmm, this mist is rather persistent today, wouldn’t you agree?” Tobin remarked, struggling to decipher a particularly perplexing section asking about the atmospheric propensity for precipitation, both expected and otherwise.

“It’s more than persistent, Tobin,” Mizzle seemed to communicate with a sharp glance. Then she trotted a few paces towards the very edge of the gorge, where the mist was thickest, and looked back at Tobin, tail giving a sharp urgent wag. Bartholomew, startled by her sudden movement, let out a shaky sigh.

“It’s them,” he whispered, voice barely audible above the wind’s low moan. “The grumbles. They’ve wandered close again, you see.”

“Grumbles?” Tobin asked, setting his quill down. “What are grumbles, Bartholomew?”

“Creatures of the mist,” Bartholomew explained, wringing his hands so vigorously his knuckles turned white. “When the mist gets this thick, especially with the wind from the north, they get confused. They wander. They make noises. And I don’t like noises, wizard. Especially when they’re near my bridge. Hence the form. To ensure no one unforeseen arrives with them and causes further trouble.”

Mizzle, with a determined glint in her amber eyes, trotted purposefully over to a cluster of large moss-covered boulders near the end of the bridge, where the mist seemed particularly dense. Tobin, trusting Mizzle implicitly, followed, his previous concern about the form entirely forgotten. Mizzle led him with a series of soft yips and pointed nudges. Peeking around a damp dripping stone, they saw them.

Three small round creatures, no bigger than plump cottage loaves, were huddled together. They were covered in soft grey downy fur that seemed to absorb the very light around them, and they had wide innocent dark eyes and tiny little button noses. They were shivering visibly, and letting out a series of soft melancholic whimpers that sounded like a forgotten lullaby sung by a lonely wind chime. And then Tobin realised, with a pang of understanding, that the Sunpetal herbs, the very reason for his quest, were growing just a few feet beyond their hiding place, nestled on a small sheltered ledge, bathed in the faint light that pierced the fog.

Tobin’s eyes softened. His heart, as vast and warm as his own hearth, felt a profound warmth spread through his chest. He was not a wizard of grand earth-shattering pronouncements, but a wizard of quiet solutions. He remembered a small charming spell, one he had learned long ago for warming cold tea on a frosty morning.

“Mizzle,” he murmured, “I believe our quest has taken a slight but important detour. These grumbles are simply lost and very frightened.”

He knelt down, magnificent beard nearly brushing the mossy ground, careful not to startle the little creatures. He held out a hand, and with a gentle lilting incantation, a soft golden light bloomed from his palm. It was not a blinding dramatic flash, but a warm comforting glow, like the first shy rays of a sunrise peeking over the mountain peaks. The grumbles blinked, their whimpers softening, wide eyes fixed on the gentle light. Mizzle, sensing their fear lessening, nudged one of the grumbles gently with her nose.

“There, there, little ones,” Tobin said in his kindest most soothing voice. “The mist will pass, and you’ll be safe. But this isn’t a very safe place for such small creatures. Come, let’s find you somewhere warmer and drier.”

With Mizzle acting as a furry four-legged shepherd, guiding them with soft nudges and reassuring soft barks, Tobin led the grumbles away from the bridge and towards a sheltered sun-warmed cave he had noticed earlier on their ascent. The grumbles, drawn by the comforting warmth of Tobin’s light and Mizzle’s calm steady presence, followed without protest, their whimpers finally ceasing.

When they returned to the bridge, Bartholomew Crumple was standing there, wiping tears from his eyes with the back of his hand. “They’re gone?” he asked, voice hoarse with a mixture of relief and disbelief.

“They are safe and warm, Bartholomew,” Tobin assured him with a gentle smile. “And the Sunpetal will be waiting for you, and for us, when you are ready to allow passage.”

Bartholomew looked at Tobin, then at Mizzle, who sat looking up at him with intelligent amber eyes, tail giving a slow contented thump. He then looked at the formidable crumpled Form 7B-gamma lying neglected on the ground. With a sigh that seemed to release all the tension that had been holding his stout frame together, he reached down and picked it up. Then, with a decisive gesture, he crumpled it into a tight ball.

“No, wizard,” he said, a small genuine smile finally gracing his lips. “No form is needed now. You’ve done more than just pass over my bridge. You’ve solved a problem that I, with all my rules and regulations, couldn’t face myself. And you, little fox,” he winked at Mizzle, who gave a dignified nod, “you’re a cleverer companion than any official document could ever hope to prove.”

Tobin, with a grateful nod, then proceeded to gather the radiant Sunpetal, its golden petals glowing even in the fading light. As they walked back across the bridge, Mizzle nudged his hand. Tobin smiled, reaching down to scratch her behind the ears. The Elderbloom brew would have sunlight in it after all, and a little leftover warmth from a cave that had never asked for a form. The mist thinned. The path ahead came back. Bartholomew, for once, did not unfold a new scroll.
characters: Tobin (a crumb-bearded planning wizard), Mizzle (an amber-eyed mountain fox)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
